finding: The normative definition of `blocking` is "no surviving non-PASS row carries a blocking severity", but the spec never states WHICH of error|warning|info are blocking. The sentence leans on "the same terms" as review_converge_on, yet review is over a different vocabulary: internal/cli/review.go:1973 defines the review rule as "critical or high severity under review_converge_on=blocking". There is no critical/high in an audit row and no mapping is given. An implementer must infer error-only from a parenthetical in the §2.1 table ("r2, r3 carry zero error") and from §7 test 2 (warning and info count clean), which is inference from examples, not a definition.
suggestion: State the set literally in §2: under blocking a non-PASS row blocks iff its severity is error; warning and info do not block. Add a named engine predicate (the audit twin of ValidReviewConvergeOn / the review blocking-severity set) so the setter, the record path and the status path read one definition.

finding: The paragraph that makes this release safe to ship is false as written. It claims severity is "already validated" and that "audit_schema.go rejects a row that omits it", so "nothing new is asserted by the agent being measured". internal/cli/audit_schema.go is a prompt generator: it writes the sentence "severity: field MUST exist; null for PASS, one of error|warning|info for PARTIAL or FAIL" into the emitted prompt and carries severity nowhere else (one occurrence, in the example row on line 17). Nothing parses or rejects it. No audit-side code reads severity at all: the only audit row predicate is engine.AuditRowIsPass, which reads status alone, and internal/engine's severity references are all review-side (reviewconvergeon.go, reviewclean.go, cluster.go, locationcluster.go, vague.go, configresolve.go) with zero occurrences in auditrounds.go, rolestreaks.go, divergence.go or speccoverage.go. So audit_converge_on turns an unvalidated string written by the agent under audit into the thing that opens the release gate, which is verbatim the objection §6 Non-Goal 1 uses to defer scope for a fourth time. The AX cost the spec has not budgeted is the validator this argument assumes: a record-path refusal, its exit code, its hint and its test are new surface, not free.
suggestion: Either add row-level severity validation on the --record path as its own budgeted task and restate §2 in terms of what actually rejects, or drop the "nothing new is asserted" argument and answer the self-declared-label objection for severity on its own merits.

finding: The release's central safety argument is factually false about the code, and this repository's own corpus refutes it. §2 says 'Audit rows carry severity from the same error|warning|info vocabulary the schema requires, and audit_schema.go rejects a row that omits it. Nothing new is asserted by the agent being measured.' Measured: internal/cli/audit_schema.go only WRITES the sentence '- severity: field MUST exist; null for PASS, one of error|warning|info' into the prompt (line 24); no code path validates it. countAuditFindings (internal/cli/audit_record.go:228-257) validates category via invalidCategoryRows and never looks at severity. Across all 10,435 recorded audit rows in spec/.tp-review/, 67 non-PASS rows carry a severity OUTSIDE the claimed enum: high 16, medium 15, low 36, in cycles 0.29.0, 0.30.0, 0.31.0, 0.31.2 and 0.32.0 (0.32.0 alone has 24 low, 6 medium, 4 high). So the field the whole release gates on is unvalidated, and the corpus already contains values `blocking` has no rule for. The irony is recorded in the code: audit_record.go:259-270 explains that invalidCategoryRows exists precisely because 'tp renders the enum into every auditor prompt ... in words that promise unknown values are rejected -- and then never looked at what came back'. §2 makes that same mistake about the neighbouring field.
suggestion: Delete the false clause. Then either (a) make it true in this release -- add a record-time severity validator mirroring invalidCategoryRows, rejecting an absent severity, a non-PASS row with null severity, and any value outside error|warning|info, with a §7 test that a bad row is refused; or (b) state explicitly how `blocking` classifies an absent, null or out-of-enum severity on a non-PASS row, and add a §7 test pinning that. Without one of the two, `audit_converge_on=blocking` has an undefined case that 67 recorded rows already occupy.

finding: The safety argument "The field it reads already exists and is already validated ... audit_schema.go rejects a row that omits it. Nothing new is asserted by the agent being measured" does not hold. internal/cli/audit_schema.go is a prompt RENDERER: renderAuditOutputSchema writes the sentence "severity: field MUST exist; null for PASS, one of error|warning|info for PARTIAL or FAIL" into the auditor prompt. It rejects nothing. The only row validation on the record path is invalidCategoryRows in internal/cli/audit_record.go, which checks `category` and nothing else, and whose own doc comment records this exact failure mode for category: tp "renders the enum into every auditor prompt ... in words that promise unknown values are rejected -- and then never looked at what came back". So a non-PASS row can reach the permanent round file with severity absent, null, or an arbitrary string, and the whole convergence decision would rest on it.
suggestion: Either add severity validation to the record path in this release (mirroring invalidCategoryRows: collect every offending line, abort with one message) and say so in §2 and §7, or state the fallback the blocking predicate applies to a non-PASS row whose severity is missing/null/unknown. Fail-closed (treat it as blocking) is the only choice that cannot be exploited by the agent being gated; whichever is chosen, name it, because the release ships nothing safe without it.

finding: §2's safety argument rests on a false code claim. It states the severity field 'is already validated' and that 'audit_schema.go rejects a row that omits it', concluding 'Nothing new is asserted by the agent being measured' — the single sentence that separates severity from the thrice-deferred scope field. Measured: internal/cli/audit_schema.go contains one function, renderAuditOutputSchema, whose doc comment reads 'renders the NDJSON output schema block embedded in every audit prompt'. Its line 24 writes the string '- severity: field MUST exist; null for PASS, one of error|warning|info for PARTIAL or FAIL' into the prompt. It validates nothing. Confirmed a second way: the token 'severity' appears zero times in internal/cli/audit_record.go, and a sweep of every production .go file under internal/ returns 171 lines, none of which is an audit-side severity check — there is no ValidAuditSeverity, and engine.SeverityRank knows only critical|high|medium|low, ranking error/warning/info alike as unknown. The contrast is decisive because tp already paid for this exact mistake with the sibling field: category IS checked at the sink by invalidCategoryRows in audit_record.go, whose own comment says it exists because 'tp renders the enum into every auditor prompt through engine.RenderAuditCategoryText, in words that promise "unknown values are rejected" — and then never looked at what came back.' §2 reads a prompt-side MUST as a validator, which is that defect's definition. Consequence for the design, not just the citation: severity on a PARTIAL/FAIL row is a self-declared judgement written by the agent whose work is being gated, with nothing to check it against — which is verbatim v0.33.0 §5 Non-Goal 1's test for why scope may not gate ('role is an attribution the sub-agent copies from the prompt tp gave it, checkable against the panel tp emitted, while a scope label is a judgement with nothing to check it against'). severity falls on the scope side of that line, not the role side, so §2's central distinction does not hold as written.
suggestion: Either (a) drop 'already validated' and make the sink check part of this release — a row whose status is PARTIAL or FAIL and whose severity is outside error|warning|info is refused by tp audit --record, mirroring invalidCategoryRows line-for-line, with a §7 test that a hand-edited row carrying severity 'trivial' or null is rejected rather than counted clean; or (b) keep severity unvalidated and rewrite §2's third paragraph to argue the gate is safe for some other reason, since the 'nothing new is asserted' reason is unavailable. Do not ship the claim as it stands: it is the load-bearing sentence of the release.

finding: §3 never says who may set a disposition, and under the mechanism tp already ships the answer is: the agent being audited. tp audit --resolve is an ordinary CLI call with no operator fence — it is not among CLAUDE.md's four user-approved decisions, and engine/nextunits.go:188 plus engine/unitkind.go:264 define an audit-fix unit whose entire durable output can be a disposition with no code change (internal/cli/audit_resolve_test.go:104-118 asserts exactly that). So under §3 a unit can converge its own phase by writing wontfix on its own findings, and under tp run nothing is watching. This is the same hazard §2 cites to defer scope a fourth time, arriving through a different door, and it is strictly worse than scope because it needs no new field to exploit.
suggestion: State who may write a disposition that stops counting. Either fence wontfix/duplicate behind the operator (an escalation or an explicit user-approved decision like --skip-gate and import --force), or restrict the exclusion to dispositions recorded outside the audited unit, and say which in §3 rather than leaving it to the implementer.

finding: §4 and §7 test 4 give different answers on this repository's own recorded data, so one of them must fail. §4 requires that a spec_hash differing from the previous round's resets the streak. Measured in spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json: audit round 8 carries spec_hash sha256:1259a4af... and round 9 carries sha256:54e031e6... -- the spec moved between the only two clean rounds of that cycle. So under §4 the streak is reset at round 9 and `all` converges at round 10, not round 9. Test 4 asserts `all` converges 'at round 9, reproducing the recorded history exactly', and §2.1 rests its opt-in argument on that same 'exactly'. With §4 active the recorded history is NOT reproduced. (v0.36.0 has the same hazard: 8 distinct spec hashes across its 13 recorded audit rounds.)
suggestion: Decide and say which rule the replay runs under. Either state that test 4's replay evaluates the severity predicate ONLY, with §4's reset explicitly out of scope for that test, and re-word §2.1's 'reproduces the recorded history exactly' to 'reproduces the recorded finding counts exactly, ignoring the §4 reset'; or keep them composed and correct the expected values to blocking=round 3 / all=round 10, adding a third test that the v0.35.0 r8-to-r9 hash change is what moves the number. Either way §4 should carry the observation that tp's own converging cycle changed its spec between its two clean rounds -- that is the release's motivating defect occurring in its own evidence.

finding: §4 falsifies §2.1's table and §7 test 4, in the same release, on this repository's own recorded data. §4 resets consecutive_clean to zero whenever tp audit --record sees a spec_hash different from the previous round's. §2.1 claims blocking converges v0.35.0 at round 3 and all at round 9, and §7 test 4 makes that replay the acceptance evidence that the change is 'opt-in rather than a silent reinterpretation'. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json, the nine audit rounds' spec hashes are r1 a46f45c6, r2 a46f45c6, r3 c06544ea, r4 50be1428, r5 2dd780c6, r6 6f42a8eb, r7 1259a4af, r8 1259a4af, r9 54e031e6 — the hash changes at r3, r4, r5, r6, r7 and r9, six of nine rounds. Under §4, r3's reset zeroes the streak blocking needed, so blocking does not converge at round 3; and r9's reset zeroes the streak r8 built, so all does not converge at round 9 either. Neither cell of the table survives the section three headings later, and 'all reproduces the recorded history exactly' — the sentence that carries the opt-in argument — is false once §4 ships, regardless of which value audit_converge_on takes. (v0.36.0 differs by luck: r2 and r3 share f7da0fde, so blocking's round-3 stop survives there.) A second, unstated cost falls out of the same measurement: the spec moved between rounds in 13 of the 22 recorded audit rounds across the two cycles, so in this repository §4's reset is the normal case, not the exception — while §7 test 8 pins only the case that does not occur ('a cycle whose spec never changes ... so the reset costs nothing when nothing moved').
suggestion: State the composition explicitly and re-derive the evidence under it. Concretely: (1) say in §2.1 whether the replay is computed with §4 active or with §4 held out, and if held out say why that is a fair test of a release that ships both; (2) re-run the table under both mechanisms and print the resulting cells, or withdraw the 'reproduces the recorded history exactly' claim; (3) add a §7 test for the case the data says is normal — a cycle whose spec moves between two otherwise-clean rounds — beside test 8's no-movement case; (4) fix the ordering for decomposition: test 4 as written is unwritable once §4 lands, so either it is written and run before §4's task, or it is restated over a fixture whose hash is held constant.

finding: Three of the seven substantive sections -- §5, §5a, §5b, roughly 100 of 288 lines -- have no entry in §7 and no entry in §6, so nothing says whether they ship in v0.37.0, and nothing could fail if they were dropped. §5 is the sharpest case: it states 'What this release must decide', then declines to decide ('The candidate shapes, neither chosen here'), and then states a test. But its two candidates are observationally different -- a `converge_roles` workflow field emits new config and changes what --check reads, whereas 'a --check that reports the shipping predicate itself with the all-roles count demoted to advisory' changes the payload shape and no config -- so two engineers implementing to §5 produce different JSON contracts and both satisfy the sentence. §5b likewise states a defect and 'the cheap answer' with no requirement, no test, and no non-goal.
suggestion: For each of §5, §5a, §5b, do one of two things and nothing else: choose the mechanism and add its numbered test to §7, or move it to §6 with the release that takes it named (§5b already points at spec/0.46.0.md §8 for provenance and could point there for delivery). If §5's choice is genuinely deferred, the honest form is a Non-Goal that says --check keeps its current all-roles meaning in v0.37.0, not a 'must decide' with no decision.

finding: §5 is titled as a defect this release must fix, says "What this release must decide", and then does not decide it: it offers "The candidate shapes, neither chosen here" -- a role-scoped convergence set (converge_roles) or a --check that reports the shipping predicate with the all-roles count demoted to advisory. These are not two spellings of one change; they differ in the config surface, the payload shape, and what exit 0 means. I cannot open a commit against this section. The acceptance sentence at the end (a fixture where the conformance role is clean while another role has open non-FAIL rows must reach exit 0) is satisfied by both shapes and by shapes neither names, so it does not close the gap either.
suggestion: Choose one shape and specify it (field name, default, payload keys, exit-code table), or move §5 to Non-Goals with a pointer to the version that takes it. A section whose requirement is "decide the design" cannot be decomposed and will be re-derived by hand in the implementation phase, which is exactly what the section complains about.

finding: Change (2), "A PASS carrying such a statement is an unresolved item for convergence, not a clean one", requires a machine-readable marker on the row, and §5a specifies none. engine.AuditRowIsPass is byte-exact (status == "PASS", "no trimming, no case folding"), so nothing in the row as it exists today can carry the statement; §5a explicitly declines to touch the checklist, and change (1) is only a wording change to the emitted brief, which produces prose in `notes` at best. Unspecified: the field name, whether renderAuditOutputSchema must require it, whether it is validated at record, whether such a row carries a severity (and therefore whether it blocks under audit_converge_on=blocking from §2), and which of the five AuditRowIsPass consumers must stop treating it as clean.
suggestion: Specify the carrier explicitly -- e.g. a nullable `unaddressed` object with the statement plus the recommendation change (1) forces -- its schema row, its validation, its severity semantics, and the predicate change (state it as a new engine predicate rather than as a change to AuditRowIsPass, whose doc comment forbids drift). Also reconcile with §6 item 5: deferring "a fourth row status" to spec/0.49.0.md §5 while requiring a PASS row to count as unresolved is the same need answered twice, in two releases, in two shapes.

finding: Rule (2) of §5a -- 'A PASS carrying such a statement is an unresolved item for convergence, not a clean one' -- has no detectable subject, and under the only field that exists today no fixture in this repository can ever produce a clean round. §5a says the two changes touch nothing on the checklist and names no field, no marker and no detection rule for 'my prose knows something my verdict cannot carry'. The only free-text field on an audit row is `notes` (audit_schema.go:25, max 500 chars, 'always'). Measured on the four rounds §5a itself cites (spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/audit-round-10..13.ndjson): 100% of PASS rows carry a non-empty note -- 82/82, 83/83, 82/82, 81/81 -- and 74/74 spec-coverage PASS rows in every one of the four. So the mechanizable reading of rule (2) makes every round unclean forever and pins spec_coverage_clean_rounds at 0 permanently. §5a's own claim 'On the second rule none of the four rounds named above was clean' is therefore true by construction and cannot fail -- it is a restatement, not evidence.
suggestion: Name the carrier and the predicate, or move rule (2) to §6. The cheap shape: a new optional row key (e.g. `unrecorded_observation`: string|null, with the recommendation required when non-null, since §5a's own fifth case shows a bare note sits unactioned) and a stated convergence rule 'a PASS row with a non-null unrecorded_observation counts as open'. Then §7 gains a test that can fail: a fixture round of all-PASS rows where exactly one carries the field is not clean, and the same round with the field null is clean. Note also that a fixture proving the OLD behaviour must exist too -- rounds 10-13 as recorded are the fixture that must stay clean under today's rule.

finding: 'blocking' is never defined for audit severities, so tests 2 and 3 cannot be written from §2 alone. §2 says blocking 'counts a round clean when no surviving non-PASS row carries a blocking severity' without ever saying which of error|warning|info is blocking. The only clue is a parenthetical in §2.1's table ('r2, r3 carry zero error') and the wording of §7 tests 2-3 -- i.e. the tests define the term the spec was supposed to define. §2 also claims audit_converge_on 'takes the same two values on the same terms' as review_converge_on; that is false at the level that matters. Review grades a 4-value scale and blocks on critical|high (internal/cli/review.go:1973: 'critical or high severity under review_converge_on=blocking'); audit grades a 3-value enum. 'The same terms' cannot hold across two different partitions of two different vocabularies.
suggestion: State the audit blocking set as a literal in §2 -- e.g. 'blocking = {error}; warning and info are advisory' -- and replace 'the same two values on the same terms' with the explicit mapping, naming that the two phases use different severity vocabularies and therefore different blocking sets. A named constant pair (AuditConvergeOnBlocking/All plus an AuditSeverityBlocking predicate) is the twin of engine/reviewconvergeon.go the section claims to be.

finding: No surface contract is given for the new field. §7 test 1 requires it to resolve "through the documented precedence", but nothing in this document documents a precedence or names a single surface. review_converge_on touches at least: engine/projectconfig.go (the allowed project-field set and its validator), cli/set.go (the settable workflow field list plus its enum branch), cli/set_project.go, cli/config.go (--resolved), cli/config_extract.go, cli/validate_project.go, engine/unattended.go (whether a raise/change is a user-approved decision under TP_UNATTENDED), and the consuming commands. v0.31.1 exists precisely because review_converge_on shipped missing config --extract and validate --project. Without the list, this release repeats that miss and the gap is invisible until a later cycle.
suggestion: Add a §2 subsection enumerating every surface audit_converge_on must appear on, with the precedence spelled out (CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in), and state whether it is a TP_UNATTENDED-guarded decision. One list makes it decomposable into one task per surface and makes the omission checkable.

finding: The default is stated as a requirement in §2 ("Default. blocking, matching review_converge_on") and then re-opened in §2.1: "whichever default ships" and "Decomposition should treat the default as the one decision in this release with a recorded argument against it". An implementer writing the built-in constant needs one answer. As written I cannot tell whether blocking is the specified default or a proposal the decomposition phase is being asked to settle, and the two produce different code, different config defaults, and a different meaning for every existing repo that upgrades.
suggestion: Pick the default in §2 and keep §2.1 as the recorded argument against it, or state explicitly that the default is `all` (behaviour-preserving on upgrade) with blocking opt-in. Either is buildable; the current pair is not. If the intent is for the operator to decide at decomposition, say so as an escalation rather than as a stated default.

finding: The release ships blocking as the default while its own §2.1 says "the two cycles disagree, and one sample each way is not a policy" and records a defect blocking would have shipped over (the WriteSnapshotAtomic fixed-.tmp collision, found at v0.36.0 round 7, four rounds after blocking would have closed the phase). A default is the one setting every project pays without reading this spec, so choosing the contested side spends the argument on everybody. §2.1 also states the cheaper alternative in the same breath: all "reproduces the recorded history exactly, which is what makes the change opt-in rather than a reinterpretation" — that property belongs to whichever value is the default, and it is discarded by defaulting to blocking.
suggestion: Default to all, which changes no existing project's behaviour and leaves blocking as the opt-in the measurement supports; or, if blocking must be the default, state the decision rule that settles a split sample rather than resting on symmetry with review_converge_on.

finding: The release turns on which audit severities block, and §2 never says. Its predicate reads 'blocking counts a round clean when no surviving non-PASS row carries a blocking severity' — a definition in terms of an undefined set. The set is recoverable only by inference, from §2.1's parentheticals ('r2, r3 carry zero error') and §7 tests 2 and 3, i.e. blocking = {error}. The review twin does not do this: v0.31.0 §4.1 states its set normatively ('The blocking severities are critical and high ... medium and low do not'), fixes it as not itself a knob, and — the half that matters more here — states the conservative rule for a severity that is missing or out of vocabulary: it is 'treated conservatively as blocking, so an ill-formed severity from an LLM reviewer never lets a genuine defect count toward convergence' (engine/reviewclean.go implements exactly that). §2 states neither, and the omission is reachable rather than theoretical: measured across this repository's v0.35.0 and v0.36.0 audit rounds, all 2913 PASS rows carry an explicit severity key whose value is JSON null, so null is a value the recorded corpus actually contains, nothing rejects it on a PARTIAL/FAIL row (see the §2 row above), and the spec does not say whether such a row blocks. Left unstated, the implementer's default — a map lookup that misses — fails OPEN, which is the direction v0.31.0 deliberately refused.
suggestion: Add a normative clause in §2 with three parts, mirroring v0.31.0 §4.1: (1) the blocking audit severity set is {error}, and it is fixed in this release rather than configurable; (2) matching is case-insensitive after trimming; (3) a non-PASS row whose severity is null, absent, or outside error|warning|info is treated conservatively as blocking. Then add a §7 test that pins part (3) specifically, since it is the one that decides whether the gate fails open.

finding: The same protected guard pins the absence of this release's central field: internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:472-474 asserts that tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking fails with "unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on", and spec/0.34.0.tasks.json recorded the handover verbatim — "should it ever arrive, that assertion is the test that has to move with it". §2 and §7 test 1 add the field without mentioning the guard, so the release opens with a known-failing protected test and no owner for it.
suggestion: Add the guard's retirement to §7 test 1 or to §2, naming the file, the test and the assertion that is replaced.

finding: §2's account of why the knob was deferred three times does not match the record it cites, and it omits the one deferral that was about severity. (1) 'The two were bundled under one heading and only one of them was risky' — they were not bundled: spec/0.33.0.md §5 lists them as separate Non-Goals 1 and 2, and Non-Goal 2's reason is a dependency, not a shared risk: 'It has no meaning without item 1.' spec/0.34.0-candidates.md §2 restates the same dependency ('Without a trustworthy scope, the knob has nothing to select on'). (2) The deferred knob is not this knob. spec/0.33.0-candidates.md §1 designs audit_converge_on as 'spec | all, default spec' — a selector over the scope field. This release proposes 'blocking | all' over severity. Those are different fields sharing a name, so 'the same objection was aimed at both' is not the right description of what happened; the honest description is that the name is being reused for a different design, which is a stronger position and should be argued as such. (3) The omission that matters: §2 cites 0.33.0, 0.34.0 and 0.35.0 and never cites v0.31.0 — the release that shipped review_converge_on and explicitly declined to mirror it into audit, for a reason about severity rather than scope. spec/0.31.0.md §4.4: 'Audit convergence is unchanged ... its error | warning | info severity is a display annotation the stop check never reads ... This release adds no severity-awareness to audit convergence and no audit_converge_on field. Audit runs to two consecutive clean rounds as before; implementation correctness is not negotiable against severity.' Non-Goal 4 repeats it and test 8 pins 'there is no audit_converge_on'. §2's claim 'That objection does not touch severity' is true of v0.33.0's objection and false of v0.31.0's, which touches nothing else.
suggestion: Rewrite the paragraph around the real history: say that the deferred audit_converge_on was a scope selector and that this one is a severity selector sharing its name; drop 'bundled under one heading'; and add a paragraph quoting v0.31.0 §4.4's actual objection — 'implementation correctness is not negotiable against severity' — and answering it. That answer is the release's real argument and it is currently missing.

finding: The table cell "v0.36.0 | 7 and open" is stale, and it understates the case against the default it is cited for. Counted just now over spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/audit-round-*.ndjson there are THIRTEEN recorded audit rounds, and non-PASS error rows appear in rounds 1 (8), 7 (3), 12 (2) and 13 (2). §5 of this same spec tabulates rounds 10-13 and §2.0a discusses rounds 12 and 13, so the document contradicts itself about how long that cycle ran. Everything else I could re-derive holds: v0.35.0 is 3 error / 22 warning / 17 info as §1 says, blocking converges at round 3 and all at round 9 under audit_clean_rounds 2, and v0.36.0 under all has still not converged at round 13.
suggestion: Refresh the cell to 13 and restate the argument on the fuller data: under blocking + 2 clean rounds v0.36.0 would have closed at round 3 and then missed error rows in rounds 7, 12 AND 13, not only round 7. Since §2.1 tells decomposition this is the one decision with a recorded argument against it, the decomposer needs the correct size of that argument.

finding: The table is presented as a measurement 'in both directions' with v0.35.0 as 'the case for the release' and v0.36.0 as the only case against. Replayed row by row against the recorded rounds, both cycles are cases against the default, and the column that would show it is the one the table omits. Per-round non-PASS severity, computed from spec/.tp-review/*/state.json and the round files: v0.35.0 r1 {error 2, warning 5, info 5}, r2 {warning 5, info 7}, r3 {warning 2, info 3}, r4 {error 1, warning 2, info 1}, r5 {warning 6}, r6 {warning 1}, r7 {warning 1, info 1}, r8 {}, r9 {}. So blocking stops that cycle after r3 — and r4, the very next round, carries an error row. §2.1 discounts two of v0.36.0's three round-7 errors as 'repair artifacts of round 6 [that] would not exist in a cycle that had stopped at round 3'; that defence is unavailable for v0.35.0's r4 error, which is one round past the proposed stop, not four. The honest score of the spec's own instrument is therefore 2 of 2 cycles in which blocking would have shipped over an error-severity row, not 1 of 2. The framing hides it because the columns ask when the loop stops rather than what was still to be found after it stopped; a third column, 'highest severity recorded after the blocking stop', reads error for v0.35.0 (r4) and error for v0.36.0 (r7, r12, r13). §2.1's closing sentence — 'the two cycles disagree, and one sample each way is not a policy' — is the sentence this row falsifies: they do not disagree.
suggestion: Add the third column and recompute the reading. Then make the default an explicit, argued choice rather than a symmetry ('matching review_converge_on, so the asymmetry disappears'): either ship all as the default and let blocking be the opt-in, which is what 2-of-2 supports, or keep blocking and state plainly in §2 that both measured cycles would have shipped over an error row and name what makes that acceptable — §2.0a's 'ask the role whether it still holds its own prior reasoning' is a candidate but is currently cited as a caveat rather than as a condition on the default.

finding: §2.1's table gives v0.36.0 as '7 and open' recorded rounds. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/state.json: 13 recorded audit rounds, files audit-round-1.ndjson through audit-round-13.ndjson, all present on disk. The same spec contradicts its own cell three times — §5's table tabulates rounds 10, 11, 12 and 13; §5b is measured 'against tp's own state at v0.36.0 audit round 12'; §2.0a cites 'v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13'. The number is not decorative: it is the denominator of the row that carries the entire case against the default, and 'round 7, four rounds after blocking would have closed the phase' reads very differently when it is round 7 of 13 rather than the open edge of 7.
suggestion: Change the cell to '13 and open'. Then re-read the sentences that lean on it: with rounds 8-13 in view, v0.36.0 recorded error rows at r7, r12 and r13, so 'that cycle's round 7 ... recorded three error rows' understates its own case — r12 and r13 carry two error rows each, and §2.0a already treats those as the release's central caveat. Bind the count to the artifact rather than restating it, e.g. 'every audit-round-N.ndjson recorded under spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/'.

finding: §2 and §3 compose in a way neither states, and the composition can disarm the release safety property. §2 blocking is a predicate over "surviving non-PASS rows"; §3 removes wontfix/duplicate rows from the count. Nothing says what happens to an ERROR-severity row dispositioned wontfix. On the natural reading it stops blocking, so an operator -- or, under tp run, the agent being gated -- converges the phase by labelling the one blocking row accepted. That is precisely the objection §2 cites to defer scope for a fourth time: "a self-declared label that gates a release is strictly worse than over-counting, because the agent whose work is being gated writes the label". A disposition is exactly such a label, and this release makes it gate.
suggestion: Decide and state the order and the limit. Options worth naming: an error-severity row cannot be dispositioned wontfix (refuse at --resolve with exit 2); or it can, but the round reports it under a distinct key (accepted_blocking) and --check still refuses; or dispositions are excluded only for non-error severities. Also state whether tp audit --resolve is a user-approved decision under TP_UNATTENDED, since v0.35.0 fences the other four.

finding: §3 overturns two standing Non-Goals and a shipped guard test, and §6 records neither. spec/0.33.0.md §5 Non-Goal 5 reads 'Auto-resolving or parking a non-spec-coverage finding. tp has no audit-side --resolve. Adding one is how a round of open findings quietly becomes a clean round', and Non-Goal 8 reads 'Anything tp stores that then clears the gate is audit_converge_on under another name, and it would arrive without the policy debate item 2 defers.' §3's mechanism — a stored wontfix or duplicate disposition excluded from the round's finding count — is precisely 'something tp stores that then clears the gate'. The prohibition is not merely prose: internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go's TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate disposes a go-safety FAIL as wontfix, re-records, and asserts 'a wontfix disposition does not clear go-safety's open finding' and then that tp audit --status --check still exits 1, 'the gate is still shut over the disposed finding'. The same test asserts 'unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on', so §2 inverts it too. §3's own framing makes the omission easy to miss: it says the exclusion happens 'on the same terms review already excludes a resolved finding', but review's terms are not these — engine/reviewclean.go excludes a finding resolved wontfix/duplicate whatever its severity, while §3 must additionally distinguish fixed, and the stored object is {status, evidence, resolved_at} (internal/cli/audit_resolve.go's disposition()) rather than a field named 'disposition'. §3 names neither the field path nor the values it reads.
suggestion: Add an 'Overturns' paragraph to §6 or §3 naming, with citations, v0.31.0 §4.4/Non-Goal 4/test 8, v0.33.0 §5 Non-Goals 2, 5 and 8, and v0.34.0 §11 Non-Goal 2 — stating for each why the reason given then no longer holds. Add a §7 test asserting the inversion deliberately, so TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate's two assertions are changed by a task that owns them rather than by whoever hits them first. And in §3, name the exact read: row['resolved']['status'] ∈ {wontfix, duplicate} excluded, 'fixed' not excluded, absent 'resolved' not excluded.

finding: §3 reverses a behaviour tp deliberately shipped and guards. internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go carries the comment "a disposition is not a way to park a finding past the gate" (:464-466) and asserts at :487 that "a wontfix disposition does not clear go-safety's open finding" and at :490 that --status --check stays shut over the disposed finding. That test, TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate, is on the protected guard list at spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md:56. §7 test 5 states the new counting rule but never says the shipped guard is retired or which assertions move with it, so decomposition will meet a red gate with no instruction.
suggestion: Name TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate in §7 (or in the section) with the exact assertions this release changes and what replaces each, so the reversal is a decision on the record rather than a test edit an implementer improvises.

finding: §3's mechanism names a vocabulary the spec never binds to a stored field, and it contradicts the shipped predicate of the same name. What tp actually writes is `resolved: {status, evidence, resolved_at}` (internal/cli/audit_resolve.go:190-199) with status restricted to fixed|wontfix|duplicate (requireResolveStatus, :227-232). §3 says only 'a row carrying a wontfix or duplicate disposition', never naming `resolved.status`, so test 5 ('a row dispositioned wontfix') cannot be turned into an assertion without guessing the key. Worse, the shipped `rowDisposed` (internal/engine/unitkind.go:246-253) is deliberately status-blind -- '_, disposed := row["resolved"]' -- so it already treats a `fixed` row as disposed, which is exactly what §3 says must NOT happen for counting. §3 does not say whether rowDisposed changes, whether the resolve/audit-fix unit predicate keeps its current meaning, or how a row whose disposition status is unreadable is treated (dispositionStatusOf, :203-210, returns the string 'unknown' for that case).
suggestion: Pin the field path (`resolved.status`), the excluded value set ({wontfix, duplicate}), and the treatment of a `resolved` object with an absent, non-string or unknown status (the conservative reading -- not excluded -- matches the rest of tp's conventions and should be stated, not inferred). Say explicitly whether engine.rowDisposed keeps its status-blind meaning for units while convergence gets a status-aware one, and if so, name both predicates so a reader cannot confuse them.

finding: The reset names exactly one counter -- "resets consecutive_clean to zero". Every other streak the loop stores is left untouched: role_streaks[].consecutive_clean and spec_coverage_clean_rounds (engine/rolestreaks.go). §5 and §5b of this same spec establish that the shipping rule people actually use reads spec_coverage_clean_rounds, so under §4 as written an agent can amend the spec mid-audit, lose the counter nobody ships on, and keep the counter everybody ships on -- which is the §1 hazard verbatim. Two further gaps: the first recorded round has no previous round to compare against (no rule stated), and the comparison is against the PREVIOUS ROUND spec_hash, so a spec that moves and moves back between two records is invisible.
suggestion: State the full reset scope: name every streak the change zeroes (or state explicitly which survive and why). Define the first-round case. If the intent is to catch the §1 case ("the spec hash changed twice mid-audit"), say whether --record compares against the previous round hash or against the live spec on disk -- they catch different things.

finding: §4's mechanism and test 6 are unwritable as assertions on four counts. (1) 'resets consecutive_clean to zero' names a quantity that is not stored: engine.ConsecutiveClean (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:429-438) recomputes live from rounds[i].Clean on every call, so there is nothing to reset -- the implementable form is a stop condition in that walk, and the two differ observably on later rounds. (2) Test 6 says the reset is reported 'on the machine-readable surface' without naming a key; every other signal in this area is a named key (required_clean_rounds, role_streaks, spec_coverage_clean_rounds, divergence), so this one must be too. (3) It does not say which surfaces report it -- only the --record payload that observed the change, or --status thereafter. (4) The existing engine.Converged already ANDs !StateStale(rounds, currentHash) (reviewstate.go:509-511), so a spec-change guard is already in the audit path; §4 does not say whether it stays, and §1's 'audit has no equivalent' is loose about that.
suggestion: Re-state the mechanism as a walk rule ('the trailing clean-round walk stops at a round whose spec_hash differs from its successor's'), name the emitted key and its value (e.g. streak_reset: {reason: "spec-changed", at_round: N} or null) and say which commands emit it, and state explicitly that Converged's StateStale term is unchanged. Then test 6 becomes an equality assertion instead of a keyword search.

finding: §5 is headed "What this release must decide" and decides nothing — "the candidate shapes, neither chosen here". The two candidates have different surfaces and different costs: converge_roles is a new list-valued workflow knob, which in this codebase means a case in each of engine/projectconfig.go, model/projectconfig.go, model/workflow.go, cli/config.go, cli/config_extract.go, cli/set.go, cli/set_project.go and cli/validate_project.go plus resolution through five layers; the alternative changes what --check means and demotes the existing all-roles count to advisory, which is a contract change for every consumer including tp run's exit-code branch. Decomposition cannot size or order the release while the choice is open, and §7 carries no numbered test for either.
suggestion: Choose one shape here, or move §5 out of this release entirely and let it ship audit_converge_on alone — the spec-length data in CLAUDE.md argues for the second.

finding: §5a rule (2) and §2 define the convergence population incompatibly, and neither section acknowledges the other. §2 states 'Both predicates are over non-PASS rows' and justifies that choice by a measurement I confirmed: across v0.35.0 and v0.36.0 every PASS row carries severity null (188/188, 195/195, ... 81/81; 0 rows anywhere omit the key). §5a then makes some PASS rows block. Such a row is non-blocking-by-construction under §2's predicate (its severity is null, which is not error, warning or info), so under audit_converge_on=blocking a PASS-with-observation is either always clean -- silently voiding rule (2) whenever the default is in force -- or always blocking, which is a fourth severity class the spec never introduces. Two engineers write opposite tests here, and one of them writes a test that passes while the mechanism it targets is inert.
suggestion: State the interaction in one sentence in §2 or §5a and test it both ways: whether a PASS row flagged under §5a blocks under `blocking`, under `all`, or both. If it should always block, say that it is exempt from the severity gate and give the reason; if it should carry a severity, say which values are legal on a PASS row and how that squares with the schema line 'severity: null for PASS'.

finding: §5a's change (2) makes a PASS row carrying a prose disclosure "an unresolved item for convergence, not a clean one", but a PASS row has no severity to classify: internal/cli/audit_schema.go:24 requires "severity: field MUST exist; null for PASS", and §2 itself records that "every PASS row carries severity: null" across v0.35.0 and v0.36.0. audit_converge_on — this release's headline mechanism and its default — is a predicate over the severity of non-PASS rows. So a disclosing PASS row is unclassifiable by the very gate shipping beside it: under blocking it can never block, under all it always does, and §5a says which in neither case. Two mechanisms in one release, and their interaction is undefined at exactly the point where both fire.
suggestion: State what severity a disclosing PASS row carries, or give the disclosure its own counter outside the severity predicate, and add the interaction (a PASS-with-disclosure round under blocking and under all) to §7.

finding: §5a's second change re-admits, under another name, the exact mechanism §2 and §6 Non-Goal 1 defer for a fourth time. '(2) A PASS carrying such a statement is an unresolved item for convergence, not a clean one' requires a new agent-written marker on a row whose presence blocks a release. §6 Non-Goal 1 defers scope because 'a self-declared label that gates a release is strictly worse than over-counting, because the agent whose work is being gated writes the label' — and that reason applies unchanged to a self-declared 'my prose knows something my verdict cannot carry' flag. §5a even supplies the aggravating detail: the note it proposes to gate on was, in its own fifth case, wrong on three of four files and had to be retracted by the same role a round later. Second, independent defect: the rule is inert under §2's own definitions. §2 fixes both predicates over non-PASS rows and defends that choice with a measurement ('every PASS row carries severity: null, so a predicate phrased over any row of any severity would read the wrong population'). A PASS row carrying a note is still a PASS row, so neither blocking nor all can see it. §5a therefore silently redefines the population §2 spent a paragraph fixing, and no section reconciles them. Under the conservative reading this review recommends elsewhere — a null severity is blocking — the reconciliation is worse, not better: every PASS-with-note row would block under blocking and not under all, inverting the two policies' strictness for that class of row.
suggestion: Pick one. Either (a) move §5a out of this release entirely — it is a finding-contract change, not a convergence-policy change, and §6 Non-Goal 5 already sends the neighbouring question ('a fourth row status') to spec/0.49.0.md §5, which is where this belongs beside it; or (b) keep it and pay its costs in full: name the new field, state in §2 that the convergence population is non-PASS rows plus PASS rows carrying that field, state how the field interacts with each of blocking and all so the strictness inversion cannot arise, answer Non-Goal 1's objection for this field specifically, and give it a §7 test. Recommendation: (a). §5a's first change — the brief asking each role to state what its row cannot carry — is cheap, non-gating, and can ship alone.

finding: §5a's two changes are in tension: (1) asks every role to volunteer what its prose knows that its row cannot carry, while (2) makes volunteering it the thing that keeps the round unclean. A role that discloses lengthens its own loop; a role that stays silent converges. Nothing can detect the omission, because the only evidence the disclosure was owed is the disclosure that was not written — so the mechanism is unfalsifiable in the direction it fails. §2.0a's own caveat depends on this working: it says a severity gate must not end rounds "which would have changed their own method", and §5a is the instrument nominated to notice that, running on an incentive that suppresses it.
suggestion: Decouple the ask from the penalty: let a disclosure be recorded without failing the round it appears in (route it to the operator or to the next round's brief), or bound (2) so only a disclosure the role itself marks as actionable blocks — and say what makes the disclosure verifiable at all.

finding: §5b measures the defect well and then states the fix as an opinion: "The cheap answer is that a recorded round should carry forward the roles it did not receive, marked as not-run rather than dropped". As a requirement it is missing every decidable part: where the expected role set comes from (the active corpus, the round roles_hash, or the previous round role_streaks), what the not-run marker is called and what an entry looks like in role_streaks, whether a round missing a role can still be clean: true, whether consecutive_clean and spec_coverage_clean_rounds freeze or reset for a carried-forward role, and what happens when the corpus itself changed between rounds (engine.ReadAuditRoundRows already drops a whole round on a differing roles_hash, so the two rules can disagree about the same round). There is also no §7 test for it.
suggestion: Promote it to a Mechanism block with the same rigour §3 and §4 get: the source of the expected role set, the literal marker, the effect on clean, on consecutive_clean, on spec_coverage_clean_rounds, and the interaction with the roles_hash rule. Add the test: a one-role round recorded against a three-role corpus leaves the other two streaks at their prior values and does not advance them.

finding: §5b's 'cheap answer' silently reverses a shipped invariant that was chosen deliberately, and its observable is unpinned, so it cannot be tested either way. The proposal is that a round 'carry forward the roles it did not receive, marked as not-run rather than dropped, so a streak can neither advance nor vanish on their behalf'. The shipped rule is the opposite by design: ComputeAuditRoleStreaks documents 'A role with no rows in a round is not clean in it: the role was not measured, so cleanliness cannot be claimed for it, and the round therefore ends that role's streak instead of being skipped over ... the conservative direction -- they reset the signal toward keep auditing rather than toward you may ship' (internal/engine/rolestreaks.go:33-40). Carrying a streak across a round that did not measure the role means spec_coverage_clean_rounds can report 3 on the strength of a round that measured no conformance at all -- which is the ship rule reading a number nothing in that round supports. §5b does not name the tension, does not say what role_streaks emits for a not-run role (consecutive_clean carried forward? open null? a new field?), and uses 'should' rather than a requirement, so a decomposer cannot tell whether it ships.
suggestion: Decide between three observably different behaviours and write the one you mean plus its test: (a) keep today's reset and instead make the ABSENCE loud -- role_streaks carries an entry {role, status: "not-run"} for every role in the corpus that contributed no rows, and spec_coverage_clean_rounds stays null, which fixes 'the role is not reported as skipped or as stale' without touching any counter; (b) carry the streak forward and state explicitly that the conservative invariant is being traded away, with the reason; (c) refuse the narrow round at record time. (a) is the smallest and contradicts nothing. Whichever ships, pin the emitted JSON, because §5b's complaint is about what the payload says, not about arithmetic.

finding: §5b's proposed fix reverses a documented contract sentence that a guard test pins verbatim, and does not say so. §5b: 'a recorded round should carry forward the roles it did not receive, marked as not-run rather than dropped, so a streak can neither advance nor vanish on their behalf.' The shipped contract says the opposite: 'A role with no rows in a round is not clean in it, so its streak ends.' That sentence is required verbatim in skills/tp/REFERENCE.md by internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go's referenceSignalSentences list, which exists (per its own comment) so 'a release that ships the fields without the wording' fails. Carrying a role forward is exactly a streak that neither ends nor advances, so the sentence and the fix cannot both stand. There is a second reason to be careful here rather than to just flip it: the current rule fails toward more auditing, which spec/0.33.0.md §1 states as a standing constraint for everything in that design ('Every rule that could fail in two directions fails toward keep auditing'). Carrying a role forward fails the other way — a role that has not been run for five rounds keeps a streak it did not earn — and §5b's own argument is that a narrow round should not read as progress.
suggestion: Name the sentence and its guard in §5b, and state the replacement wording that REFERENCE.md must then carry. Then prefer the fail-toward-auditing shape over carry-forward: report the missing role explicitly (a not_run marker in role_streaks, and spec_coverage_clean_rounds unchanged rather than nulled when the role was simply not part of the round), while keeping the rule that a not-run role's streak does not advance. That answers §5b's actual complaint — a narrow round silently setting the ship-rule quantity to null — without granting a role credit it did not earn.

finding: No test asserts that every consumer of audit convergence reads audit_converge_on, which is the failure mode §5 is complaining about. Its twin has at least five consumers -- internal/cli/review_record.go:45, internal/cli/review_status.go:36, internal/cli/budget.go:18, engine.ReviewConverged (internal/engine/reviewclean.go:130-136) and the resume/run oracle -- and audit today routes through a different, severity-blind pair (engine.Converged / engine.ConsecutiveClean, internal/engine/reviewstate.go:429-511) whose doc comments say in as many words 'audit sequences keep using ConsecutiveClean' and 'audit convergence keeps using Converged'. Tests 1-3 as written are satisfied by wiring audit_converge_on into --record alone, leaving `--status --check`, `tp resume`'s oracle and `tp run`'s stop reasons blocking on advisory rows -- i.e. the release ships and the operator still cannot ship on --check.
suggestion: Add a test that sets audit_converge_on=blocking on a fixture whose only non-PASS rows are warning/info and asserts the SAME verdict from every surface: tp audit --record's payload, tp audit --status, tp audit --status --check's exit code, and tp resume's phase. List the consumers in §2 so decomposition produces one task per surface rather than one task for the predicate.

finding: Tests 2, 3 and 5 all assert one surface and can pass while the counter the release's own §5 and §5b say the shipping rule reads stays broken. The same non-PASS predicate feeds two independent consumers: countAuditFindings (internal/cli/audit_record.go:248) produces the round's `findings`/`clean`, and auditRoundOpenByRole (internal/engine/rolestreaks.go:128-142) produces role_streaks[].open, which SpecCoverageCleanRounds reads to emit spec_coverage_clean_rounds. AuditRowIsPass's doc comment (internal/engine/auditrounds.go:43-46) states that the two 'must stay identical ... were the two to drift, the per-role open counts and the round's own stored findings would disagree about the same rows'. §3 changes only 'the round's finding count' and §2 speaks only of a round being clean. So an implementation that excludes a wontfix row from `findings` while role_streaks still counts it open passes test 5 exactly as written, and a round can report clean:true under `blocking` while spec_coverage_clean_rounds is 0 because spec-coverage's open count still includes three warnings -- which inverts §5's whole complaint instead of fixing it.
suggestion: Extend tests 2, 3 and 5 to assert the paired observable: for the same fixture round, `findings`/`clean` AND role_streaks[].open AND spec_coverage_clean_rounds must all agree about the same row. State in §2 and §3 whether the severity gate and the disposition exclusion apply to the per-role open counts too; if they deliberately do not, say so and amend AuditRowIsPass's doc comment, because it currently forbids that drift.

finding: The eight tests cover §2 (1-4), §3 (5) and §4 (6-8). §5, §5a and §5b — three of the six substantive sections, including both mechanisms that change what counts as a clean round — have no numbered test. §5's acceptance is prose inside §5 ("the test is the one v0.36.0 would have failed"), which is where an implementer will not look, and §5a's two changes and §5b's carry-forward have no acceptance anywhere. A section with no acceptance is prose that costs review rounds and produces no surface, which is the exact non-converging shape §2.0a describes.
suggestion: Give §5, §5a and §5b a numbered test each — promoting §5's inline fixture description into the list is the cheapest of the three — or drop the sections from this release.

finding: §1 closes 'This release gives audit the two things review already has: a severity-aware convergence policy, and a reason to distrust a streak that spans a changed spec.' The body ships at least five distinct mechanisms: audit_converge_on (§2), disposition-based exclusion from the finding count (§3), the spec-change streak reset (§4), a change to what --status --check measures (§5), a new gating marker on PASS rows plus a prompt change (§5a), and a change to how a round records roles it did not receive (§5b). The a/b suffixes make §5a and §5b read as facets of §5, but their subjects are three different things — which rows the gate reads, what a row can carry, and which roles a round contributes — with no shared fix and no shared test. This is worth raising as a structural finding rather than an editorial one because this repository has measured the cost: CLAUDE.md records spec length as the strongest single predictor of cycle length across fifteen cycles (r ≈ +0.56; under 200 lines ≈ 8-9 rounds, over 300 ≈ 23), and the release-splitting rule it derived — 'if a piece can be released independently, it is its own release'. At 288 lines with three sections still lacking a mechanism or a test, this spec is already on the expensive side of that line and will grow when they are supplied.
suggestion: Split. §2 + §3 + §4 is a coherent, independently releasable ~150-line spec: one policy field, one counting rule, one reset, eight tests, all three with mechanisms today. §5 + §5a + §5b is a second release about what quantity the gate should read and what a round records — and it is not ready, since §5 has no chosen mechanism, §5a needs a finding-contract change §6 Non-Goal 5 already routes elsewhere, and §5b reverses a pinned contract sentence. If the split is refused, at minimum rewrite §1's closing sentence to enumerate what actually ships, and renumber §5a/§5b as §6/§7 so the suffixes stop implying they are one topic.

finding: The error paths carry no exit codes or hints, which the review twin does specify by having two distinct ones. For review_converge_on: a bad literal at the setter exits 2 with engine.ReviewConvergeOnHint (cli/set.go, cli/set_project.go), and a resolved-but-invalid STORED value at a consuming command exits ExitValidation=1 with the same hint (cli/review_record.go:49, cli/review_status.go:40). §7 test 1 covers only "an illegal literal is refused with the hint naming both legal values" -- the setter half -- so the stored-value half of the twin would ship untested and undefined. Nothing in §3, §4, §5a or §5b names an exit code either.
suggestion: Add an exit-code line to §2: bad literal at set / set --project exits 2; an invalid stored audit_converge_on at tp audit --record / --status exits 1; hint text is the shared AuditConvergeOnHint naming blocking and all. Add the second case to test 1.

finding: The spec never says whether the emitted auditor prompt learns the active policy. The review side does: cli/review.go:1969-1973 renders one blockingRule sentence describing BOTH settings into the prompt. Two consequences if audit does not. The auditor keeps assigning severity with no idea it now gates the release, which is the moment severity stops being an unforced label and starts being one the measured agent has an incentive to lower -- the exact objection §2 uses to keep scope deferred. And §2.0a asks for a role that can be told to re-examine its own prior reasoning rather than stop at round 3, which is a prompt change nobody has been assigned.
suggestion: State whether the audit prompt carries the stop rule, and if it does, render it for both settings the way review does (one sentence, policy-independent, so prompt text does not vary with a workflow field). Say explicitly whether §2.0a caveat produces any prompt change in THIS release or is only a note pointing at spec/0.49.0.md §1c.

finding: The one stated safety condition on the contested default has no mechanism in this release and is delegated to a spec that does not exist yet. §2.0a says a severity gate 'must not become a default stop at round 3 that ends rounds which would have changed their own method', cites v0.36.0 rounds 12 and 13 as the case (I confirmed: 2 error rows in each, on a cycle whose spec-coverage role had been clean since round 10), and then answers it by pointing at spec/0.49.0.md §1c. Per CLAUDE.md's own release plan 0.49.0 is last of thirteen and still pre-design. So the release ships a default whose stated precondition is owned by nothing, is in no §6 Non-Goal, and has no test. A 'must not' with no owner is the shape a later cycle re-derives from scratch.
suggestion: Either accept the risk in §6 explicitly ('this release ships blocking knowing it would have stopped v0.36.0's audit before rounds 12-13; the mitigation is spec/0.49.0.md §1c and is not part of v0.37.0'), or ship the cheap in-release mitigation and test it: when a round converges under blocking with non-blocking rows still open, --check and --record say so on the machine-readable surface (a nonblocking_open count and the roles carrying them), so the stop is visible rather than silent. The second is testable this cycle; the first at least stops the condition from reading as a requirement nobody implemented.

finding: A disposition is written by tp audit --resolve into the results NDJSON, which normally happens AFTER the round was recorded; the round finding count is frozen at --record time. §3 does not say whether the exclusion is applied when the round is recorded (so a row accepted afterwards never unblocks the round it was found in -- the field-cycle scenario §3 exists to fix) or recomputed from the current results files at --status/--check time (which is what the review side does: review_status.go recomputes survivors under the "current resolution" state). §7 test 5 passes under either reading, so the ambiguity survives the test.
suggestion: State the evaluation time explicitly and mirror review if that is the intent. If it is recompute-at-status, say what --record stores in findings so the stored number and the reported number are not silently different quantities.

finding: §3 scopes the change to "the round finding count" only. But AuditRowIsPass has five call sites and its own doc comment makes the identity load-bearing: "This is byte-for-byte the predicate the audit record path applies ... it must stay identical to it: were the two to drift, the per-role open counts and the round stored findings would disagree about the same rows." The consumers are cli/audit_record.go:248 (the count), engine/rolestreaks.go:138 (per-role open + streaks), engine/divergence.go:137 (the divergence signal), and engine/nextunits.go:188 (which ALREADY excludes disposed rows via rowDisposed). Excluding wontfix/duplicate in the count alone breaks the stated invariant; excluding it everywhere silently changes divergence, the one signal §1 credits with catching this class.
suggestion: Enumerate the consumers and state for each whether the disposition exclusion applies. In particular say what divergence should see: an accepted-backlog row is precisely the input divergence was built to notice, so hiding it there may be the wrong half of the fix.

finding: "and says so in the payload" (§4) and "reports the reset on the machine-readable surface" (§7 test 6) name no key, no value, and no command. tp audit has two machine-readable surfaces (--record and --status), and the reset is a fact both would want. An implementer will invent a key name; a later cycle will find it undiscoverable, exactly as §5 describes for the --check gap.
suggestion: Name the key and its value (e.g. streak_reset_reason: spec_changed with the two hashes), say which surfaces carry it (--record, --status, or both), and say whether it changes the exit code of anything. Then test 6 becomes assertable as written.

finding: §4 opens 'audit has no equivalent', and that is not accurate as stated. engine.Converged is `ConsecutiveClean(rounds) >= requiredCleanRounds && !StateStale(rounds, currentHash)`, and StateStale compares the spec on disk against the LAST RECORDED ROUND's spec_hash — so a spec amended after the last recorded round already blocks convergence today, on both review and audit, and divergence condition 3 reads the same flag. What audit genuinely lacks is only the between-rounds case: a spec amended, then a fresh round recorded against the new text, which restores !StateStale while the earlier rounds in the streak were read against different bytes. §4 should claim that narrower gap, because as written it invites an implementation that duplicates a guard tp already has. The section also introduces a third hash comparison without relating it to the two that exist — StateStale (disk vs latest round), RolesStale (current corpus vs latest round's stored roles_hash), and now §4's (this round vs previous round) — and states no precedence among them or what --status reports when two disagree. Finally, §4 removes an asymmetry a prior release states as deliberate: spec/0.33.0.md §1, 'The two staleness axes are deliberately not symmetric — a corpus change ends the streak, a spec change only has to be absent at the moment of reporting.' §4 makes the spec axis end the streak too, which may well be right, but it is an overturn and is not recorded as one.
suggestion: Narrow the opening claim to the between-rounds case and say what Converged/StateStale already covers. Name all three comparisons in one place with their precedence and their reported fields. Add a sentence overturning spec/0.33.0.md §1's asymmetry explicitly, with the reason it no longer holds. And state the boundary case §4 leaves open: what happens on the FIRST recorded round, where there is no previous round to differ from.

finding: §4's rule is pairwise ('a spec_hash different from the previous round's') and three edges it must decide are unstated, one of which is the loophole its own threat model describes. (a) Amend-then-revert: hash A -> B -> A. Under the pairwise rule the streak resets twice; under a 'count only rounds carrying the current spec_hash' rule the pre-change rounds resurrect and the streak survives. §1's stated threat is 'an agent can amend the spec to match code it just wrote and keep its clean-round streak', and revert-after-record is the cheapest way to do exactly that, so the two readings differ precisely where it matters. (b) The first recorded round has no predecessor -- reset or not. (c) §4 says the reset and spec/0.45.0.md's --reconcile 'compose' and that neither is a prerequisite, but not whether a reconciled move still resets; a reader can take 'reconcile explains the change' as 'reconcile excuses it'.
suggestion: State the rule over the whole recorded history rather than pairwise, add the first-round case in one clause, and add a §7 test for the A -> B -> A sequence with the expected streak value spelled out. On --reconcile, one sentence: a reconciled change resets the streak exactly as an unreconciled one does (the reconcile record is for the reader, not for the counter) -- or the opposite, if that is the intent, but it must be written.

finding: Both candidate shapes lean on "the conformance role" -- converge_roles "defaulting to the conformance role", and a --check reporting "conformance-role streak plus no-FAIL". tp has no notion of a conformance role: roles are user-defined files under .tp/auditors/, per-spec activation has existed since v0.32.0, and spec_coverage_clean_rounds is already a signal keyed to one literal role name that a corpus need not contain. The spec never says how the role is identified, nor what --check does in a corpus with no spec-coverage role (every field repo that ejects or renames the corpus), nor what happens when the named role is deactivated for this spec.
suggestion: State the identification rule and the fallback: an explicit configured role list with no name-based default, or a documented default of spec-coverage plus the defined behaviour when it is absent or inactive (fall back to all roles, or refuse with an exit code and hint). This is the part a field repo hits first.

finding: converge_roles is proposed "defaulting to the conformance role", but tp has no general notion of one. engine.RoleSpecCoverage is the literal string spec-coverage, and role corpora have been fully user-defined since v0.26.0, so the default names a role that exists only in corpora that happen to use tp's own name for it. Every other project either sets the knob or gets a default matching nothing, and the spec does not say what --check does when the named role is absent from the corpus — which is the case that decides whether the gate fails open or closed.
suggestion: State the default as the literal spec-coverage and specify the absent-role behaviour explicitly, or derive the convergence set from the corpus (roles whose checklist covers spec sections) so no per-project knob is needed.

finding: §5 is headed 'What this release must decide' and then declines to decide: 'The candidate shapes, neither chosen here.' The two candidates are not variants of one design — the first adds a new workflow field (converge_roles) with its own resolution precedence, validation, config --resolved surface and staleness interaction; the second changes the meaning of an existing exit code on --status --check and demotes the all-roles count to advisory, which is a contract change to an output every CI wired to tp reads. They differ in surface, in blast radius, and in which of §6's Non-Goals they brush against. A section in this state cannot be decomposed into tasks with acceptance, and the release cannot state its own exit-code contract.
suggestion: Choose before decomposition, and say which on the evidence: the exit-code reinterpretation is the smaller change but silently alters what an existing green CI means, while converge_roles is additive and leaves today's --check meaning intact for anyone who does not set it. If the choice cannot be made in this cycle, make §5 a Non-Goal pointing at the release that decides it, and keep §2/§3/§4 — that is a coherent release on its own. What must not happen is decomposition starting with §5 unresolved, because §5's shape decides whether §2's audit_converge_on is read by --check at all.

finding: §5 pins its fixture on a status vocabulary the rest of the release does not use, so two engineers build different fixtures. The row vocabulary is PASS|PARTIAL|FAIL (audit_schema.go:20). §2, §3 and the whole counting mechanism are phrased on non-PASS; §5's test says 'another role has open non-FAIL rows'; and the CLAUDE.md rule §5 is reconciling with is phrased on a third quantity, 'no round has produced a FAIL'. A PARTIAL row is non-PASS and non-FAIL at once, so 'open non-FAIL rows' is satisfiable two ways and the exit-0 expectation differs between them. Worth recording that the fixture itself is producible -- v0.36.0 rounds 10-13 are literally it: spec-coverage open=0 for four consecutive rounds while maintainability-conventions carries 2/1/2/3 open rows, all PARTIAL or FAIL, and I reproduced §5's table exactly from those files -- so this is a wording defect, not a missing-fixture one.
suggestion: Rewrite §5's test on one vocabulary: 'the conformance role has zero non-PASS rows for required_clean_rounds consecutive rounds while another role has at least one non-PASS row'. Then say separately whether the shipping predicate's 'no FAIL' half is part of what --check would report, since that half is about status FAIL specifically and is the one place the two vocabularies genuinely both appear. Use spec/.tp-review/0.36.0 rounds 10-13 as the named fixture -- it is committed, it is the case the section argues from, and it costs nothing to construct.

finding: §5's first candidate is 'a role-scoped convergence set (converge_roles, defaulting to the conformance role)', and 'the conformance role' is not a general tp concept — it is a hardcoded id. engine/rolestreaks.go: `const RoleSpecCoverage = "spec-coverage"`, with the comment 'the only role in the corpus that measures spec conformance', and engine.SpecCoverageCleanRounds returns nil unless a streak entry's Role equals that literal byte-for-byte. Auditor corpora are user-defined (.tp/auditors/*.json) and, since v0.32.0, per-spec deactivatable; tp's own corpus contains spec-coverage only because tp chose to name it that. So in a project whose corpus has no role with that exact id — or a spec that deactivates it — spec_coverage_clean_rounds is permanently null, and a --check defaulting to 'the conformance role' has no quantity to read. §5 states no rule for that state, which means the release's own gate would fail open or shut with nothing in the spec deciding which. §5b's transcript shows the same null arriving from a different direction, so this is not a hypothetical corner.
suggestion: State the absent-role rule normatively in §5: when converge_roles resolves to a set no role in the active corpus satisfies, --check must refuse rather than pass (fail toward keep-auditing, per spec/0.33.0.md §1's standing constraint) and must say which configured role ids were not found. Better still, key the default off the corpus rather than a literal — the role carrying the spec-derived checklist — and if that is not derivable today, say so and keep the literal with the refusal rule attached.

finding: §5a's first change — 'The brief asks each role to state anything its prose knows that its row cannot carry, and to say what should be done about it' — is a change to the emitted audit prompt, and it lands on structures the suite pins verbatim. internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go pins two prompt orders as required substrings: specCoverageOrder = 'Role → Role Rules → Spec Excerpt → JSON-array Checklist → Affected Files → Output Schema' and sharedArmOrder = 'Role → Role Rules → Project Context → JSON-array Checklist → Disposition → Affected Files → Output Schema'. Neither has a slot for a new block. The arm that matters is the one with less room: internal/cli/audit_roles.go renders the Disposition block only `if role != roleSpecCoverage`, so spec-coverage's prompt has no precedent for a block between the checklist and the affected files — and every one of §5a's five measured cases is a spec-coverage row. So the new clause must reach the arm the existing per-arm split excludes, and §5a says only 'the brief' without naming the position, the arm, or the documents that carry the order.
suggestion: Name the position in both orders and update both pinned strings in the same task, or attach the clause to the Output Schema block (which both arms already render) rather than adding a seventh section. Either way say explicitly that the clause reaches spec-coverage, since that is the arm the section's own evidence comes from and the arm the current per-role split would skip by default.

finding: §5a(1) adds a standing clause to every role's brief in every round, paid roles x rounds, for an event measured five times across two repositories. tp's own v0.36.0 is an entire release about what the emitted prompt costs, and this release adds to it without a byte budget. The spec also does not say whether the clause is emitted to every role or only to roles whose rows can be PASS, nor whether --role emission carries it, nor whether it survives --compact — each of which is a per-field decision this repo asserts in tests elsewhere.
suggestion: Bound the ask: emit the clause only where it can fire (a role whose rows are all PASS, or a round that would otherwise be clean), and state its emission and --compact disposition the way §2.4 of spec/0.33.0.md states the signal fields.

finding: §5 and §5b have a hard ordering dependency that neither states. §5 proposes moving --check onto the conformance role's streak; §5b measures that the same quantity is silently set to null by a round recorded with one role, reports it as clean:true, and notes this is newly easy — 'v0.36.0 shipped --role, which makes a one-role round easy to run for the first time, and the interactive fallback runs exactly one role per unit.' If §5 lands first, the release moves the release gate onto a counter it has, in the adjacent section, just documented as erasable by the workflow this repository actually runs. §6 and §7 state no ordering, and §7 has no test for either section, so nothing in the spec prevents the tasks being scheduled in that order.
suggestion: State in §5 that §5b is a prerequisite: --check may not be re-based on the conformance streak until a round that did not receive a role can no longer null it. If only one of the two can ship this cycle, ship §5b — it is a defect with a measured reproduction, while §5 is still choosing a mechanism.

finding: §5b's "cheap answer" stores a not-run marker per absent role on every recorded round. tp already has everything needed to derive that set at read time: each recorded audit round stores a roles_hash, and the audit outputs already read the live corpus and compare against it (engine.ComputeRolesHash, divergence condition 5, roles_stale). The roles a round did not receive is the corpus role set minus the roles present in that round's rows — computable from data already on disk, with no new stored bytes per round, and it stays correct when the corpus changes, which a frozen stored marker will not.
suggestion: Derive the not-run set at read time from the corpus and the round's rows; if a stored marker is still wanted, state what it buys over the derivation and what happens to it when the corpus changes underneath it.

finding: Half the spec's normative sections have no test. Tests 1-4 cover §2, test 5 covers §3, tests 6-8 cover §4. §5, §5a and §5b — three sections that between them change what --check measures, what makes a round clean, and how a round's roles are recorded — carry none. §5 is the sharpest case because it does state its test, in prose, and that test never reaches §7: 'the test is the one v0.36.0 would have failed: a fixture where the conformance role is clean for required_clean_rounds running while another role has open non-FAIL rows must reach exit 0, and must not reach it if the conformance role has an open row.' A test stated in a body section and absent from the Tests section will not be decomposed: tasks take source_sections, and the section that owns the behaviour is not the section a test task would be pointed at.
suggestion: Either promote the prose tests into §7 — §5's exit-0/exit-1 fixture pair, §5a's 'none of the four rounds named above was clean' as a replayable assertion, §5b's one-role round preserving rather than nulling the counter — or move §5, §5a and §5b out of this release. Leaving them normative-but-untested is the option to avoid: it is what lets an implementer close the release with §2, §3 and §4 done and three sections silently unimplemented.

finding: Test 1 cannot be written deterministically: neither the precedence layers nor the exit code is pinned, and its twin has two different refusal paths with two different codes. 'Resolves through the documented precedence' does not say which layers apply -- review_converge_on has no CLI flag and no env var; it is settable at the task layer (internal/cli/set.go:45,371-376) and the project layer (internal/cli/set_project.go:64-69) only, so the generic CLI > env > task > project > built-in chain has two live layers here and three inapplicable ones. And 'an illegal literal is refused with the hint naming both legal values' collapses two shipped behaviours: tp set rejects a literal with ExitUsage/2 (set.go:374-376), while a CONSUMING command rejects an already-stored illegal value with ExitValidation/1 (review_record.go:45-49, review_status.go:36-40). Both are 'refused with the hint'; they are different tests.
